content:
The defunct Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China (the Alliance) and its former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan, former vice-chairs Albert Ho and Chow Hang-tung are charged with "inciting subversion of state power." The Alliance, Lee and Chow pleaded not guilty. The case was handed down today (the 21st) at the West Kowloon Court. National security designated judges Victor So, Andrew Chan and Alice Lai ruled that the Alliance, Lee and Chow were guilty, and adjourned the case to next Friday (the 28th) for sentencing submissions. While the judges were delivering the verdict, Chow Hang-tung smiled briefly, while Lee Cheuk-yan took off his glasses and gazed at the judges with a calm expression. After the judges finished reading the verdict and announced they would retire, Lee turned back and laughed at the correctional services officers. When the court rose, Lee Cheuk-yan smiled at his relatives and friends, placed his hands above his head to form a large heart shape, and bowed. His wife Tang Yin-yee and Ventus Lau also placed their hands above their heads to form a large heart shape in response. Since the case was charged in September 2021, spanning nearly five years, Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung have been denied bail throughout and have been remanded for over 4 years and 11 months. Albert Ho, who was once granted bail, has also been remanded for over 4 years and 4 months, awaiting sentencing after the verdict. Related reports: Alliance Case Verdict – Outside the Court | A woman reportedly taken away for clothing deemed to have seditious intent; police barred Tang Yuet-kwan from bringing "June Fourth" reports into court. Alliance Case – Verdict | How did Chow Hang-tung spend five years in prison? Friend Ventus Lau: Do what should be done, uphold the righteousness that should be upheld. Alliance Case – Verdict | The family's "lively spirit" lost freedom for over five years; Lee Cheuk-yan lost his mother while in prison, missed his beloved daughter's wedding; drew paintings for his wife, conveying longing.

The public gallery in the main courtroom is full. Most people are wearing masks. Security personnel asked some people wearing caps to remove them.

Most people in the public gallery of the main courtroom wore masks. National security police entered the courtroom to hear the verdict.

All 65 seats in the public gallery of the main courtroom are full. The vast majority of people wore masks, and several people wore caps but were asked by security to remove them after entering the courtroom. Chow Hang-tung's mother, Lee Cheuk-yan's wife Tang Yin-yee and her sister Tang Yin-lei, former Alliance standing committee member Ventus Lau, defendants released in the 47 Case Wu Man-yee and Shiu Ka-chun, social activist "Big Yellow Uncle," and "Long Hair" Lei Yu-lin attended the hearing. Police Deputy Commissioner (National Security) Kan Kai-yan, Assistant Commissioner (National Security 1) Wong Chung-fun, and Chief Superintendent of the National Security Department Li Kwai-wah all entered the courtroom and sat behind the Department of Justice to hear the verdict.

When the court clerk distributed copies of the summary of the verdict to the journalists present, Tang Yin-yee (in the picture) once asked: "Is there one for family members? What do family members get?"

Lee Cheuk-yan waves as he enters the courtroom; Chow Hang-tung flashes a toothy smile

At about 9:53 am, the two were escorted into the courtroom by multiple correctional officers. Lee Cheuk-yan, with grey hair, wearing a white top and blue windbreaker, waved and smiled at his relatives and friends, and also waved at his lawyers. Chow Hang-tung, wearing glasses and her hair in a long ponytail, a black top and an off-white long coat, flashed a toothy smile at her relatives and friends. After communicating with the lawyers, the two sat down in the dock, guarded by eight correctional officers. Chow Hang-tung communicated with her relatives and friends through lip reading across the distance.

Consuls of various countries stationed in Hong Kong heard the verdict in the extension courtroom. Several regular court observers entered Extension Courtroom No. 2 to listen to the hearing, including "dentist" Li Ying-chi, Big Yellow Uncle, and "Ma Si Po Uncle Chan." Some court observers said after hearing the verdict, "Man proposes, God disposes." Others shed tears, saying that they had been coming to hear the hearings over the past few years, and felt sad and distressed upon hearing the verdict of "guilty" today. They also felt helpless about being unable to enter the main courtroom today, questioning whether those people know nothing about the case details or even received benefits. She continued that she had participated in the Victoria Park gatherings back then, hoping the defendants would know that there are always people "standing by" them.

Before entering the courtroom, a citizen raised a V-shaped gesture symbolizing the Alliance's emblem.

Judges rule the charges established

At the opening of the hearing, Judge Victor So stated that the reasons for the verdict totalled 206 pages plus attachments, and that he did not intend to read them all out. He indicated that after announcing the verdict the court would retire, and the court clerk would then distribute the written reasons for the verdict.

Victor So subsequently read out the verdict, ruling that the prosecution had proven beyond reasonable doubt that during the offence period, Chow Hang-tung and Lee Cheuk-yan incited others to overthrow the fundamental system established by the Constitution, with the intent and belief that those being incited would act as they were incited, with the purpose of subverting state power led by the Chinese Communist Party, and ruled the two defendants guilty. Victor So continued that the two were the "directing minds" of the Alliance, and based on the "doctrine of attribution," treated the unlawful intent and conduct of the three defendants that had been established to be related to the charge as the intent and conduct of the Alliance, ruling the Alliance guilty, and announcing that the court would retire.

After the judge announced "proven beyond reasonable doubt," Chow Hang-tung flashed a brief toothy smile, then looked calmly toward the judge. Lee Cheuk-yan also took off his glasses and looked at the judge with a calm expression. After the judge announced that the court would retire, Lee Cheuk-yan turned his head back and laughed at the correctional officers. When the court rose, Lee Cheuk-yan smiled at his relatives and friends, placed his hands above his head to form a large heart shape, and bowed. His wife Tang Yin-yee and Ventus Lau also placed their hands above their heads to form a large heart shape in response.

Chow Hang-tung's mother attended the hearing today.

Adjourned to 8.28 for sentencing submissions

After a recess of about 30 minutes, Victor So adjourned the case to 10 am on August 28 for sentencing submissions. The defence's written submissions are to be filed by next Wednesday (the 26th). He also stated that he did not expect the prosecution to make submissions on sentencing, and quipped, "I suppose when it comes to case law, we only have those few cases – Lui Sai-yu, Gordon Ng (47 Case), Ma Tseun-man – they are all very familiar to us." Unless the prosecution thinks of others, no special assistance is required.

However, Victor So pointed out that the offence of inciting subversion of state power has a two-tier sentencing system: 5 to 10 years' imprisonment for serious cases, and under 5 years for less serious cases, and hoped the defence could provide assistance on "how this case should be categorised." When the court rose, Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung waved and smiled at their relatives and friends, with Lee using his arm to make a heart shape.

Judge: Under the Constitution, there is no possibility of Western-style party rotation

The court ruled that, based on the preamble and Article 1 of the Constitution, it is indisputable that "the socialist system is the fundamental system of the People's Republic of China," and that "the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party," as "the most essential feature" of socialism with Chinese characteristics, is an indispensable element of the "fundamental system." The various democratic parties "participate in" the patriotic united front led by the CCP, therefore the CCP's leadership as the ruling party is established and guaranteed by the Constitution, and there is no possibility of Western-style party rotation. Therefore, under the current Constitution, "overthrowing" or "undermining" the leadership of the CCP is equivalent to "overthrowing" or "undermining" the "fundamental system" established by the Constitution as referred to in Article 22 of the National Security Law.

Judge: The goal of ending one-party dictatorship is ending CCP leadership

The court ruled that "ending one-party dictatorship" does not mean asking the CCP to return to a multi-party cooperation system under the Constitution, but rather ending its leadership, and that "ending" clearly does not mean "natural conclusion," but carries the meaning of "overthrowing" and "undermining." The court also ruled that the Alliance's standing committee (including the three defendants) understood this. The court ruling stated that the three defendants, both in their personal capacities and as Alliance standing committee members, actively promoted and carried out activities related to the action programme of "ending one-party dictatorship," targeting primarily people in Hong Kong, as well as those participating in their activities and browsing the Alliance's website.

The court also ruled that a reasonable person generally (especially one living in Hong Kong), upon receiving messages about "ending one-party dictatorship" from the Alliance and the three defendants, would inevitably understand that the goal was to end the leadership of the CCP, and would also certainly understand that each defendant was encouraging others to take action to end the CCP's leadership.

The court ruled that the three defendants had consistently harboured hostility toward the CCP and the central government it leads, and had adhered to a line of confrontation with and no compromise toward the central government. The court added that the three defendants did not believe that in the hostile atmosphere they had created, there was any possibility of peaceful dialogue with the central government.

Consuls of various countries stationed in Hong Kong heard the verdict in the extension courtroom.

Judge: After the National Security Law, refused to rein in at the brink, persisted in their own way

The court ruling pointed out that, given that domestic dissidents had been jailed because of the Charter 08 movement, and because the three defendants believed there was no possibility of peaceful communication between the Alliance and the central government, the court found that the defendants did not believe that amending the Constitution to achieve "ending one-party dictatorship" was a practically viable means, nor was it what they sought.

The court ruled that after the implementation of the National Security Law, the defendants did not genuinely believe that their words and deeds did not violate the National Security Law, but refused to rein in at the brink, stubbornly holding the Alliance's resistance stance through to the end. The court also stated that it had not overlooked the fact that Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung had not put forward any concrete implementation methods or timetable for putting "ending one-party dictatorship" into practice, but pointed out that each defendant continued to advocate and promote "ending one-party dictatorship" after the implementation of the National Security Law, deliberately drawing parallels between the June Fourth incident that occurred more than 30 years ago and the "anti-extradition"风波, using this to provoke hostility toward the Communist Party among the audience, thereby eroding and destroying public confidence in the Communist Party.

Alleged Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung provoked hostility and division, causing loss of trust in the Communist Party

The court ruled that even though the Alliance had never adopted or advocated violence, or threatened to use violent means, after the implementation of the National Security Law, the three defendants still adhered to the platform of "ending one-party dictatorship," disregarding the fact that the platform violated the Constitution as amended in 2018, constituting "other unlawful means" within the offence of "subversion of state power" under the National Security Law.

The court ruled that Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung attempted to achieve the goal of undermining the "fundamental system" by provoking hostility and division, causing others to lose trust in the Communist Party. The court also ruled that the three defendants intended to encourage Alliance supporters to bide their time and use unlawful means to implement "ending one-party dictatorship," and that resistance acts, even if not involving violence or threats of violence, would violate the National Security Law and carry the risk of prolonged imprisonment. The court ruled that the three defendants knew that their words and deeds might exceed the scope of lawful freedom of expression, and did not care at all.

The court ruled that the three defendants intended and believed that if the audience acted on their incitement, the latter would use unlawful means, namely means violating the Constitution and the National Security Law, for the purpose of subverting state power led by the CCP.

Based on the above factual findings, the court ruled that the acts of Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung constituted a "prohibited act (i)," that is, overthrowing or undermining the "fundamental system" established by the Constitution, with the related intent. As for "prohibited act (ii)," that is, overthrowing "central authorities," the court held that it had to be considered separately and independently from "prohibited act (i)," and ruled that the prosecution ultimately had not provided sufficient evidence to prove it.

Defendants acted with the Alliance's "directing mind"

Regarding the Alliance, the court stated that the three defendants were Alliance standing committee members during the offence period, and as standing committee members, they must have served as Alliance directors. Based on the defendants' evidence, when disputes arose, the standing committee would handle them by vote, and the court accepted that the standing committee's decisions were decisive and binding.

During the offence period, the three defendants issued statements related to "ending one-party dictatorship" and participated in related activities in their capacity as Alliance standing committee members. The court stated that there was no doubt that each of them acted with the Alliance's "directing mind and will," distinct from the Alliance's employees or agents. Based on the "doctrine of attribution," the court treated the unlawful intent and conduct of the three defendants that had been established to be related to the charge as the intent and conduct of the Alliance, and therefore ruled the Alliance guilty.

Inciting subversion of state power – 5 to 10 years for serious cases

The Alliance, along with Lee Cheuk-yan, Chow Hang-tung and Albert Ho, are charged with one count of "inciting subversion of state power," alleging that they incited others to carry out "acts aimed at subverting state power" by "unlawful means," namely overthrowing or undermining the fundamental system of China established by the Chinese Constitution, or overthrowing the central authorities. The prosecution defined "unlawful means" as "ending the leadership of the Chinese Communist Party, in violation of the Chinese Constitution (particularly Article 1 and the preamble)."

Under the National Security Law, a conviction for inciting subversion of state power carries 5 to 10 years' imprisonment for "serious cases," and under 5 years' imprisonment, detention, or restriction for "less serious cases."

Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung were refused bail and have been remanded throughout this case, while Albert Ho was once granted bail but had his bail revoked about 7 months later on allegations of breaching conditions. Lee and Chow have now been remanded for over 1,800 days, and Albert Ho for nearly 1,600 days. Counting from Lee Cheuk-yan's imprisonment in April 2021 for the 8.18 rally case, he has now been deprived of liberty for over 5 years and 4 months.

The core of this case revolves around whether "ending one-party dictatorship," one of the "Five Major Platforms" used by the Alliance for over 30 years, involves inciting subversion of state power. The prosecution alleged that this amounted to "ending Communist Party leadership" and overthrowing or undermining the fundamental system of the state, constituting incitement to subvert state power by "unlawful means." However, the defence rebutted that "ending one-party dictatorship" merely meant ending the unlawful "party dictatorship" and building a democratic China, not equivalent to ending Communist Party leadership. The defence said the defendants had no hostility toward the CCP and no intent to subvert, and the prosecution failed to point to what actions the Alliance encouraged people to take to "end one-party dictatorship."
